common_name: Profusion Cherry Zinnia (AAS-Winning Original Disease-Resistant Single Zinnia)

planting.note: Wait until soil has warmed after the last frost date before direct sowing; Profusion Cherry was one of the two original 1999 AAS Gold Medal colors that launched the whole interspecific Profusion line.

directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep directly in the garden once the soil has warmed, or set out young transplants; established plants need no staking and shrug off the heat and humidity that stall most bedding annuals by midsummer. Profusion Cherry carries the vivid magenta-red single blooms that, alongside Profusion Orange, made zinnia breeding history as the first AAS-winning interspecific hybrid, prized for compact mounded growth and strong resistance to powdery mildew and leaf spot. Deadheading is unnecessary since spent flowers detach cleanly as new buds open in a continuous cycle from late spring through the first hard freeze. Group plants closely for a dense flowering hedge in beds or containers where regular tall zinnias would need constant disease management.

common_name: Profusion Apricot Zinnia (Compact Disease-Resistant Single Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow once nights stay reliably warm; Profusion Apricot forms a wider mound than most Profusion colors, so give it a bit more elbow room at planting.

directions: Direct sow shallowly in full sun after danger of frost, or transplant seedlings started a few weeks earlier indoors. Profusion Apricot produces soft coral-orange petals surrounding a deeper terracotta center disk, on a wide, well-branched mound that spreads noticeably broader than it grows tall, making it useful for filling landscape gaps quickly. Like the rest of the series it tolerates prolonged heat and drought once established and resists the powdery mildew and leaf spot that plague standard garden zinnias in humid regions. Light, infrequent watering and occasional feeding are all it needs to bloom nonstop into fall.

common_name: Profusion Fire Zinnia (Scarlet-Orange Disease-Resistant Single Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost in full sun; Profusion Fire was a standout in the Dallas Arboretum's summer heat trials, making it a reliable pick for the hottest gardens.

directions: Sow seed directly in well-drained garden soil after the last frost, spacing plants to let air move freely through the foliage. Profusion Fire opens bright scarlet-orange single flowers with a frilled golden-brown center on compact, tidy mounds, holding color intensity even through peak summer heat that fades many other bedding annuals. The plant's dense, self-cleaning habit means old blooms drop away on their own, keeping the display tidy without deadheading. It performs equally well massed in landscape beds or grown in containers, and its heat tolerance makes it a dependable choice where summer temperatures regularly climb into the 90s.

common_name: Profusion Coral Pink Zinnia (Compact Disease-Resistant Single Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost; this was one of the newer color additions to the Profusion line, bred to extend the series' pink-to-salmon range.

directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep once the soil has warmed, or plant nursery starts after frost danger has passed. Profusion Coral Pink covers its low, bushy mound nonstop with 2-inch single flowers in a bright coral-pink shade brushed with hints of salmon and orange, giving a softer color note than the series' hotter reds and oranges. It shares the family's strong resistance to powdery mildew and leaf spot along with a self-cleaning habit that keeps the plant looking fresh without deadheading. Its compact size suits edging, mixed containers, and mass landscape plantings where a dependable, weather-tough bloomer is needed all summer.

common_name: Profusion Double Hot Cherry Zinnia (AAS-Winning Fully Double Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost into full sun; Profusion Double Hot Cherry, a 2013 AAS winner, adds a fully double flower form to the series' signature disease resistance.

directions: Direct sow shallowly after the last frost, or set out transplants into well-drained garden soil in full sun. Profusion Double Hot Cherry produces fully double, ruffled blooms in a saturated cherry-red that hold their form and color through a long, hot growing season, an AAS-recognized advance over the series' original single-flowered types. The compact, mounding plants need no pinching or staking and drop spent flowers cleanly, keeping the bed tidy with no deadheading required. Expect strong resistance to powdery mildew and leaf spot along with steady bloom from late spring through the first fall frost.

common_name: Profusion Double Golden Zinnia (Fully Double Disease-Resistant Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost; this broad, wide-spreading double selection benefits from slightly more spacing than the single-flowered Profusion colors.

directions: Sow seed directly into warm garden soil after frost danger passes, or transplant started seedlings, spacing generously since this selection spreads wider than it grows tall. Profusion Double Golden bears fully double, rounded blooms in rich golden-orange tones, giving a rose-like texture that stands out among the series' mostly single-flowered members. It carries the same heat tolerance and strong resistance to powdery mildew and leaf spot that define the Profusion line, blooming continuously without deadheading through the hottest months. Use it in mass plantings, borders, or large containers for a long season of dense, weather-tough color.

common_name: Zahara Fire Zinnia (Large-Flowered Disease-Resistant Single Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost; Zahara Fire's single flowers run noticeably larger than comparable Profusion colors, so give plants a bit more room to display them.

directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep after the last frost, or set out transplants into full sun once nights have warmed. Zahara Fire opens single, fiery red-orange flowers roughly 2.5 to 3 inches across — noticeably larger than the equivalent Profusion colors — on a bushy, well-branched mound with clean, disease-resistant foliage. No deadheading is needed since spent blooms fall away as fresh buds continue to open through the season. It tolerates heat, humidity, and drought with ease, making it a strong candidate for landscape mass plantings where lower water use is a priority.

common_name: Zahara Yellow Zinnia (Large-Flowered Disease-Resistant Single Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost; Zahara Yellow was notable as one of the first true yellow selections in this class of interspecific zinnia.

directions: Direct sow shallowly once the soil has warmed, or plant nursery starts after frost danger has passed; light is not required for germination, so seed can be covered lightly. Zahara Yellow produces bright, glowing yellow single flowers on a dense, mounding plant, standing out as one of the earliest true-yellow introductions in the disease-resistant marylandica hybrid class. It shares the series' excellent tolerance for heat, drought, and humidity along with strong resistance to leaf spot and powdery mildew that keeps foliage clean through summer. Plant it in mass landscape beds or containers for season-long color with minimal watering once established.

common_name: Double Zahara Cherry Zinnia (AAS-Winning Fully Double Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost; Double Zahara Cherry, a 2010 AAS winner, brought a fully double flower form to the Zahara series alongside Double Zahara Fire.

directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep after the last frost, or transplant seedlings into full sun with good air circulation. Double Zahara Cherry bears large, fully double, ruffled flowers in a deep cherry-red, an AAS-recognized addition that gave the Zahara series its first double-flowered forms alongside Double Zahara Fire. Plants keep the series' dense, mounding, self-cleaning habit, so old blooms drop away without deadheading as new flowers continue to open. Expect the same reliable resistance to leaf spot and powdery mildew that lets Zahara selections thrive through humid summer conditions that damage standard garden zinnias.

common_name: Zahara Raspberry Lemonade Zinnia (Mixed-Color Disease-Resistant Landscape Blend)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost; this PanAmerican Seed color blend combines Zahara Coral Rose, Yellow, and Starlight Rose in one seed packet for varied color in a single planting.

directions: Sow seed directly in the garden after the last frost, or plant transplants into full sun; because the mix combines several distinct colors, plant it in drifts rather than single rows for the most natural-looking color blend. Zahara Raspberry Lemonade is an official PanAmerican Seed blend of the Coral Rose, Yellow, and Starlight Rose selections, giving a lively mix of pink, gold, and bicolor blooms on plants that share the Zahara series' large flower size and dense, mounding habit. All three component colors carry the same strong resistance to powdery mildew and leaf spot and the same self-cleaning, deadhead-free bloom habit. It performs best in mass landscape plantings where the mixed colors can show off together, and tolerates heat and drought with only moderate watering.

common_name: Zahara Sunburst Zinnia (Fleuroselect Gold Medal Golden-Yellow Bicolor)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost; Zahara Sunburst earned a Fleuroselect Gold Medal in Europe for its distinctive aging color pattern and disease resistance.

directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep after the last frost, or set out transplants into full sun with room to reach their taller-than-average mature height. Zahara Sunburst opens golden-yellow single flowers roughly 2.5 inches across that develop distinctive red petal stripes as the blooms age, giving the plant a two-toned look over its bloom cycle — a trait that earned it a Fleuroselect Gold Medal in Europe. The taller, upright habit compared to other Zahara colors still holds up well without staking, and the plant carries the series' strong resistance to leaf spot, powdery mildew, heat, and drought. Grow it in beds, borders, or large containers for a long season of shifting color with minimal maintenance.
